title: Where do you want me to look? Project 0 becomes three scenes
introduction: This week was crit week. On Tuesday Boyd spent the whole class teaching us how to do a crit, and after class he looked at my Project 0 page and gave me one piece of advice that changed the whole project. On Wednesday I rebuilt the page as three scenes. The crit itself is on Thursday, and on Friday the whole class goes to Bristol for the day. The first six minutes of Tuesday’s class were Boyd helping everyone book the train: the 7:18 from Southampton, back the same evening, with Teresa meeting us there. He booked my ticket himself and will email it to me. It is my first trip out of Southampton since I arrived, and I am looking forward to it more than I expected. (Thursday’s crit and the Bristol day will be added to this post afterwards.)
related_work:
Boyd taught us Liz Lerman’s Critical Response Process [1]. It has four steps: first the audience gives statements of meaning (what was strong, what stayed with you), then the artist asks questions, then the audience asks neutral questions, and only at the end are opinions allowed, and only if the artist says yes. The rule that stuck with me is that everyone must speak to every presenter: “better to be wrong than silent”. We practised on Boyd’s AR glasses. I said they looked “cute”, and he asked me what made them cute. I had to point at the blue colour and the style. Pointing at what actually works is harder than it sounds.

The crit is graded half on technique (the code, the choice of animation, the colours, how it works on different screen sizes, how AI was used) and half on meaning (how the research leads to the story). So I also looked again at my sources. Material Focus reports that millions of disposable vapes are still binned every week in the UK, and that battery fires in bin lorries and waste sites are rising [2]. That fact became the ending of my page.
method:
After class I showed Boyd my page. He said the content was fine, but the balance was off: “Equal text, equal image. Where do you want me to look? Make this really big. Right now it is spread out.” He was right. Everything on my page was the same size, so nothing led the eye.

So I rebuilt it as three scenes in one HTML file. Scene one: you take the vape apart and read a fact for each part. Scene two: you meet a person. Six frames tell the story (ten cigarettes a day, quitting, a “healthier” one, the first puff, three thousand puffs a day, can’t stop), one line each, then a button appears. Every press is one puff: the page flips black and white for a moment, smoke comes out, the battery drops, and the mood goes up and then sinks back down on a mood curve. When the battery is empty the person throws the vape away. Scene three: the thrown vapes fall into a heap, and after five of them the heap catches fire.

The biggest change is colour. In the first version I had given every part its own colour just to tell them apart; there was no design thinking behind it. Now the whole page is black and white, and the fire at the end is the only colour on the page. One thing stands out, which is exactly what Boyd asked for. I kept the original colour drawings in a backup folder, and the black-and-white versions were made with a small script that fills each part black and keeps a one-pixel white outline.

For the character I had to decide between drawing eight frames by hand and using AI. I wrote the storyboard myself (eight actions: holding a pack, throwing the pack, holding a vape, raising it, puffing and smiling, puffing and low, puffing with a flat face, throwing the vape) and the prompt, and generated the frames with Jimeng AI. Then I cut them into one sprite strip, 1416 × 280 pixels per frame, and show one frame at a time. I also traced one frame by hand in Piskel, 1,314 pixels, so I know what the full set would have cost me in time. Most of the character frames, the smoke, the fire, the parts and the pixel vapes in the pile are my own drawings; the eight character line drawings are AI, from my storyboard.
results_discussion:
The technique is the same as last week, used in new places. Switching scenes is just adding and removing one class: CSS hides every section with display: none, and the one with the class “on” is shown. The Back and Next buttons in the corners call the same function with the number before or after. The character strip works like the smoke and fire sprite sheets: the background is eight times wider than the box, and one CSS variable, --f, picks the frame; JavaScript only changes that number. The fall of a thrown vape is a CSS transition on transform, like the parts moving apart in scene one. The flash is one line: body.flash { filter: invert(1); }.

Two things were new for me. The mood curve runs on setInterval: every half second the mood sinks a little toward a floor, and that floor gets lower with every puff, so the more you puff the lower you end up. The curve itself is drawn on a canvas with lineTo. And the pile uses createElement: JavaScript makes one new image each time, gives it the class “dead”, and CSS drops it.

I also found a bug that taught me something about order. I added a shortcut so that index.html#pile jumps straight to the last scene. The first time, the scene was empty, because the jump ran at the top of the file before the script had looked up the elements it needed. Moving those two lines to the end of the file fixed it. Scripts run from top to bottom; you cannot use a name before it exists.
conclusion_future_work: The crit is on Thursday. Before that the site has to be on GitHub and linked from this portfolio, and I want to practise saying which research led to which design decision, because that is what the crit asks for. The main thing I learned this week is that hierarchy is a design decision, not decoration: one page, three scenes, one thing to look at in each, and the only colour is the ending.
references:
[1] Lerman, L. and Borstel, J. (2003) Liz Lerman’s Critical Response Process. Takoma Park, MD: Dance Exchange. https://lizlerman.com/critical-response-process/

[2] Material Focus (2024) Battery fires in bin lorries and at waste sites reach an all-time high, reported by letsrecycle.com, 13 May 2024. https://www.letsrecycle.com/news/material-focus-reports-71-increase-in-battery-fires-since-2022
